The minimum area is π/6, so a = 1, b = 6 and 100a + b = 106. I did not rigorously rule out points outside the square; I assumed the region where all four angles exceed 60° lies inside the square.

**Setup.** Γ must contain every point P where all four angles ∠APB, ∠BPC, ∠CPD, ∠DPA exceed 60°. So the minimum circle is the smallest circle enclosing that region.

**The region.** For P inside the square, ∠APB > 60° exactly when P lies inside the circle through A and B whose inscribed angle on that side is 60°. That circle has radius 1/√3, and its center lies a distance 1/(2√3) inward from side AB. The region is therefore the intersection of four such disks, one per side.

**Coordinates.** Put the square's center at the origin. The four disk centers are (±c, 0) and (0, ±c), with c = 1/2 − 1/(2√3), and each has radius r = 1/√3.

**Vertices of the intersection.** By symmetry the corner points lie on the diagonals. Take the point (t, t) on the boundary of the disk centered at (0, −c):

t² + (t + c)² = r².

This gives t = 1/(2√3). The corner points are therefore at distance √2·t = 1/√6 ≈ 0.408 from the origin.

**Farthest points.** The arc midpoints are at distance r − c ≈ 0.366 from the origin, which is less than 0.408. So the farthest points of the region are the four corner points, which lie on a circle centered at the origin. That circle is the minimum enclosing circle, with radius² = 1/6.

**Area.** The minimum area is π/6.

ANSWER: 106
